script.title: Digital Arrest Scams: Will Banks Refund Your Paisa?

segments.text: A fake Supreme Court notice just drained eighty lakh rupees from a retired teacher in Pune.

Cyber criminals set up fake police studios, put victims under so-called 'digital arrest' for days, and siphon off life savings. But now, the Supreme Court and the Reserve Bank of India are asking a brutal question: why should ordinary citizens bear the full loss when banks fail basic verification?

In the next eight minutes, we unpack the hidden business machinery behind digital arrest scams, how thousands of fake bank accounts slip past banking security, and exactly what new RBI compensation rules mean for your hard-earned money.
Here is the chilling truth: digital arrest is not some random prank call, it is a multi-million-dollar corporate enterprise running on industrial precision.

A call lands on your phone with an automated voice claiming a parcel containing narcotics was intercepted at Mumbai customs in your name. Within minutes, you are shifted to a video call where men dressed in official uniforms sit in front of authentic-looking police emblems, threatening you with non-bailable warrants.
segments.broll: man in uniform sitting at desk

segments.text: To prove your innocence, they instruct you to transfer your liquid funds to a 'clearing RBI verification account'. The victim panics, moves their entire fixed deposit, and within three minutes, that money evaporates.

Indians lost an estimated one hundred and twenty crore rupees to digital arrest scams in just the first quarter of 2024 alone. That equals the price of sixty lakh cutting chais wiped out into thin air every single month.
Now ask yourself: where does that scammed money actually land the moment you click send on your banking app?
It does not instantly fly to an overseas hacker. It enters a genuine savings account registered at a reputable commercial bank right inside India.
These are called mule accounts. Syndicates hire local agents to open accounts using forged identity papers or by bribing vulnerable people in small towns with a one-time fee of two thousand rupees.

Once your eighty lakh rupees hits a mule account, automated scripts immediately slice it into forty micro-transfers of two lakh rupees each, dispersed into separate tier-two mule accounts across five different states. By the time a panicked victim dials the 1930 cyber crime helpline, that money has already been converted into cash at local ATMs or bought as cryptocurrency on offshore exchanges.
Here is where the business economics get deeply uncomfortable for Indian banking.

When an account that usually maintains a balance of five hundred rupees suddenly receives twenty-five lakh rupees and empties it within four minutes, algorithms should scream fraud. Yet repeatedly, transactions pass through with zero human intervention or account freeze.
Banks operate under intense pressure to minimize customer drop-offs and maximize UPI transaction volume, often cutting corners on real-time transaction monitoring.
If you enjoy understanding how the real business world works behind headlines, take a quick second right now and subscribe to Paisa Decoded.
For years, banks deflected liability by pointing to OTP authentication, claiming the user authorized the transfer willingly. But the Supreme Court of India is challenging this convenient shield.
Can a commercial bank simply shrug off responsibility when their KYC systems let a ghost account steal your life savings?
The Supreme Court recently observed that RBI rules must obligate banks to fully compensate victims of digital arrest if the bank failed in proper Know-Your-Customer due diligence.

Under existing RBI circulars, if you report unauthorized electronic transactions within three working days, your zero liability is clear. But in digital arrests, the victim is coerced into hitting transfer themselves, creating a legal grey zone that left thousands bankrupt.

The apex court's strict stance forces banks to treat mule account creation as institutional negligence. If a bank opened an account with fake biometric data or ignored rapid transaction layering flags, they could soon be legally on the hook to refund the defrauded customer.
While legal protections tighten, prevention is still the only foolproof guarantee for your wealth.

Remember two basic facts: Indian law enforcement, customs, or court judges never conduct interrogations over Skype, and they never ask you to park money in a 'safe government verification account'. There is no such thing as an official digital arrest in Indian criminal law.

If you or your parents ever face this situation, disconnect immediately and dial the government cyber helpline at 1930 within the golden hour to freeze the beneficiary account. Note that this breakdown is for educational purposes only and not financial advice.
The rules of banking accountability are shifting rapidly across India, but understanding the system is your first and strongest line of defense.
